course_title: Short-Reach Optical Interconnects for AI Scale-Up Fabrics
course_subtitle: From copper reach limits to integrated optical architectures for multi-rack accelerator Pods

sources.title: OCP Short Reach Optical Interconnect Workstream

term_glossary.tooltip: Short Reach Optical Interconnect: the system-defined optical regime for intra-rack and inter-rack links up to 30 meters in an AI Pod.
Single-mode fiber: optical fiber designed to carry one spatial mode, minimizing modal dispersion.
Multimode fiber: optical fiber that carries multiple spatial modes and is commonly used for short-reach links.
Extra-short reach: an electrical interface class for package-scale paths measured in millimeters to centimeters.
Very-short reach: an electrical interface class spanning short chip-to-module or board-level paths.
Short reach: a link class extending beyond package-scale electrical paths while remaining within a system or rack-scale channel.
An optical reach class commonly specified for links up to 500 meters, where channel attenuation and optical signal quality matter.
An optical reach class commonly specified for links up to 2 kilometers, where dispersion and link margin become important.
A generic processing unit for AI workloads, such as a CPU, GPU, NPU, or TPU.
A self-contained accelerator compute domain whose processors, memory, networking, and infrastructure operate as one scalable unit.
Tightly coupled interconnect using coherent or load/store semantics within an accelerator compute domain.
The number of endpoints or links a switch or topology can connect; it constrains Pod size and hop count.
Recovering and retransmitting a digital signal to restore timing and signal quality, with added power and latency.
Failures in time: the number of failures expected per billion device-hours.
Forward error correction: coding that allows a receiver to correct certain transmission errors without requesting a retransmission.
Cyclic redundancy check: an error-detecting calculation used to determine whether a received data block contains an error.
Bit-error rate: the fraction of transmitted bits received incorrectly, commonly measured before or after forward error correction.
Signal-to-noise ratio: the strength of a desired signal relative to total noise; higher SNR provides more receiver decision margin.
Relative intensity noise: laser-output power fluctuations normalized to average optical power; at high received power, RIN can limit BER improvement.
Intensity modulation with direct detection: an optical method that encodes data in optical power and detects that intensity without coherent phase recovery.
Linear pluggable optics: a serviceable pluggable module with linear transmit and receive paths rather than full retiming.
Near-package optics: optical engines placed close to the ASIC but not on the same package.
Co-packaged optics: optical engines integrated on the same package or substrate as the ASIC.
Optical circuit switching: programmable fiber-level paths that do not electrically terminate the optical link inside the switch.
Pulse-amplitude modulation with four signal levels, carrying two bits per symbol.
Wavelength-division multiplexing: carrying multiple optical wavelengths on one fiber to increase aggregate bandwidth.

slides.title: The Scale-Up Fabric Becomes the Compute Bottleneck
slides.subtitle: Distributed training converts accelerator communication into a first-order performance constraint.

bullets.text: Tensor, pipeline, data, expert, and context parallelism distribute one model across many accelerators.
Collectives create sustained elephant flows carrying gradients, activations, and model state.
Any link bandwidth or latency shortfall leaves expensive accelerators waiting for data.

figure.alt: Silent animation of four parallel training streams crossing a scale-up fabric, one path falling behind, the synchronized accelerator group waiting, and computation recovering
figure.caption: The scale-up fabric sits directly in the critical path between parallel work and useful accelerator cycles.

slides.title: Scale-Up Is Not a Shorter Scale-Out Network
slides.subtitle: The two fabrics move different kinds of data under different timing constraints.

slides.title: Radix Converts Link Bandwidth into Pod Size

figure.alt: Diagram showing switch I/O bandwidth divided among links to determine supported accelerator count
figure.caption: For fixed switch I/O, wider links improve accelerator-to-accelerator bandwidth but reduce the number of accelerators the switch can connect.

slides.title: Copper Reach Becomes a Structural Constraint
slides.subtitle: A topology that fits one rack stops fitting when the Pod crosses rack boundaries.

bullets.text: Passive copper at 200G-class lane rates is typically limited to about 1-1.5 m.
Practical cable routes between nearby racks can require 3-7 m.
Scale-up domains of roughly 500-1,000 or more accelerators require multi-rack connectivity.

figure.alt: Single-rack copper Pod expanding into multiple racks connected by optical links
figure.caption: Optics becomes an architecture requirement when the compute domain grows beyond the reach of its copper backplane.

slides.title: SROI Defines a Distinct ≤30-Meter Optical Regime

figure.alt: Reach spectrum from electrical XSR and VSR through SROI to optical DR and FR
figure.caption: Within SROI, fiber loss and dispersion recede as design priorities; endpoint density, energy, cost, latency, and reliability take over.

slides.title: Reach, Radix, and Semantics Define the Regime
items: Scale-up performance directly controls accelerator utilization.
Load/store semantics make latency and retries unusually expensive.
Radix trades per-link bandwidth against the number of connected accelerators.
Copper reach no longer matches the geometry of multi-rack Pods.
SROI defines a common ≤30 m optical layer for multiple protocol families.

slides.title: Check Your Model: Why SROI Exists
slides.subtitle: Submit both questions for feedback. Correct answers are not required, and retries are available.

questions.prompt: What most directly distinguishes SROI from DR or FR optical reach classes?

choices.text: Its design is dominated by endpoint integration, density, power, latency, cost, and reliability
It requires more chromatic-dispersion compensation than FR
choices.feedback_incorrect: At 30 meters or less, chromatic dispersion is not the dominant constraint. Endpoint integration and system metrics define SROI.

choices.text: It is tied to one scale-up protocol
choices.feedback_incorrect: SROI is intended as a reach-defined physical layer that can aggregate volume across multiple protocol families.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. SROI optimizes the link endpoints and the full system rather than long-channel impairments.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the change in dominant constraints at 30 meters and below.

questions.prompt: Which characteristics belong to the scale-up domain?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Scale-up combines tight coupling, memory semantics, very high bandwidth, and very low latency.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Scale-up is the tightly coupled compute domain. Long-reach general networking belongs to another tier.

slides.thank_you_message: Nice work — you've finished Module 1: Why Scale-Up Needs a New Optical Reach Class.

slides.title: Finding the Copper-to-Optics Crossover
slides.subtitle: Loss budgets, reach, retiming, optical placement, and adoption thresholds.

slides.title: Architecture Boundaries You Will Locate
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module, you will be able to…
objectives: Trace the topology and reach ladder from package escape to adjacent racks.
Explain how loss budget and retiming change feasible copper reach.
Compare optical-engine placement as a change in the electrical boundary.
Interpret the paper's power, cost, latency, reliability, density, and radix targets.

slides.title: The Reach Ladder Runs from Package to Adjacent Rack

figure.alt: Reach ladder from co-packaged copper through backplane, active copper, and adjacent-rack optical links
figure.caption: The boundary is not one fixed number: package escape, board loss, connector loss, cable route, and conditioning determine where copper stops being practical.

slides.title: At 212.5 Gb/s, Every Decibel Limits Reach
slides.subtitle: Higher Nyquist frequency makes ordinary board and cable loss increasingly expensive.

slides.title: Retiming Trades Power and Latency for Reach and Robustness
slides.subtitle: More regeneration can improve margin, but the scale-up lane count multiplies every penalty.

cards.title: Non-retimed
cards.body: Lowest power and latency. Demands the cleanest electrical path and tighter system integration.

cards.title: Half-retimed
cards.body: Regenerates one direction or function. Balances margin, power, and implementation complexity.

cards.title: Fully retimed
cards.body: Strongest isolation and repair flexibility, but roughly 3-4× the power of a non-retimed path and more latency.

slides.title: Optical-Engine Placement Moves the Electrical Boundary

figure.alt: Silent animation moving an optical engine inward within a server or switch tray, from front-panel through connector-adjacent, near-package, and co-packaged positions, while the electrical path to an XPU or switch ASIC shrinks
figure.caption: Moving optics toward the ASIC shortens the lossy electrical path and improves efficiency, while making field repair more involved.

slides.title: Four Metrics Determine Broad Optical Adoption
slides.subtitle: These targets describe the system bar, not a transceiver specification.

slides.title: The Crossover Is a System Boundary
items: Passive copper remains strongest inside its natural reach envelope.
Board, package, connector, and cable losses consume one shared channel budget.
Retiming can extend reach but adds power, latency, cost, and error opportunities.
Moving optics toward the ASIC improves electrical escape at a serviceability cost.
Adoption depends on whole-system power, cost, latency, reliability, and density.

slides.title: Check Your Model: Reach and Placement
slides.subtitle: Submit both questions for feedback. Correct answers are not required, and retries are available.

questions.prompt: Which connection is most likely to require optics at 212.5 Gb/s?

choices.text: A 5 m routed connection between adjacent racks
A short co-packaged copper path inside one assembly
choices.feedback_incorrect: Co-packaged copper minimizes the electrical path and is the most favorable copper topology.

choices.text: A 1 m backplane channel with carefully managed loss
choices.feedback_incorrect: The paper shows that a well-designed same-rack channel can remain feasible near this reach.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. A 5 m adjacent-rack route is beyond the likely 2.5-3 m active-copper ceiling.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Compare the required route with the paper's passive and active copper reach ranges.

questions.prompt: Which factors can shift the copper-to-optics crossover?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The crossover is a whole-channel calculation shaped by loss, conditioning, and physical route.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Focus on elements that consume loss budget, add conditioning, or change the physical distance.

slides.title: Engineering for Reliability at Pod Scale
slides.subtitle: Link errors, hardware failures, temperature, repair, diagnostics, and resiliency.

slides.title: Failure Consequences You Will Evaluate
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module, you will be able to…
objectives: Explain why multiplying conventional optical modules fails the rack power and reliability budget.
Separate transient link reliability from repair-required hardware reliability.
Interpret FIT targets and the infant, random, and wear-out failure regimes.
Connect temperature, laser strategy, diagnostics, redundancy, and placement to Pod availability.

slides.title: A Naive Optical Substitution Fails the Rack Budget

figure.alt: 72 accelerators multiplying into 1,296 optical modules, nearly 16 kilowatts, and about 100,000 FIT
figure.caption: A component that looks acceptable alone can become unacceptable when a scale-up rack requires more than a thousand of them.

slides.title: Link Reliability and Hardware Reliability Fail Differently
slides.subtitle: Both reduce useful computation, but they demand different mitigations.

cards.title: Link reliability
cards.body: Random or burst errors, FEC-tail events, retries, and link flaps reduce effective bandwidth and add tail latency.

cards.title: Hardware reliability
cards.body: Underperforming or dead lanes require diagnosis, replacement, or architectural failover before the Pod can return to service.

slides.title: Every Retry Taxes Synchronous Compute

bullets.text: Forward error correction repairs correctable errors; a CRC checks the resulting transfer.
An uncorrectable event triggers a negative acknowledgement and retransmission.
The transaction waits for a full round trip, reducing effective bandwidth across synchronized work.

figure.alt: Silent animation of protected data passing through FEC and CRC, receiving an acknowledgement, then encountering a residual error, retrying, and stalling useful compute until recovery
figure.caption: The cost of an error is not only the bad transfer; it is the time the tightly coupled computation waits for recovery.

slides.title: The Reliability Target Approaches Silicon

figure.alt: Bathtub curve showing infant, random, and wear-out failure regimes with screening and qualification controls
figure.caption: Process screening suppresses infant failures, qualification pushes wear-out beyond service life, and the remaining random rate must approach a silicon-class floor.

slides.title: Temperature and Lasers Set the Reliability Floor

bullets.text: Optical-component FIT rises exponentially with junction temperature; the paper sets a ≤40 °C goal.
Multiple lasers compound the total random failure contribution of an optical endpoint.
External laser sources improve replaceability; on-board redundancy can reduce failure impact.

figure.alt: Reliability comparison between 70 degree and 40 degree optical operation plus external and redundant laser strategies
figure.caption: Cooling and laser architecture change the achievable reliability floor before any repair process begins.

slides.title: Repair, Diagnostics, and Redundancy Must Be Co-Designed
slides.subtitle: Behind-panel efficiency is useful only when the system can isolate and survive faults.

cards.title: Repair path
cards.body: Front-panel modules are field replaceable; NPO and CPO can require board, package, or factory-level service.

cards.title: Diagnostics
cards.body: Fault isolation must distinguish electrical from optical and near-end from far-end failures quickly.

cards.title: Resiliency
cards.body: Spare lanes and components can preserve service, but correlated failure modes reduce the theoretical benefit.

cards.title: Qualification
cards.body: Behind-panel optics may need a higher bar than conventional pluggables because repair halts valuable compute.

slides.title: Availability Is an Architectural Property
items: Module count multiplies component power and failure rates into system-level consequences.
Transient link errors consume bandwidth and create tail latency through retries.
Hardware reliability must approach a ≤2 FIT per optical-end target.
Lower temperature and a deliberate laser strategy improve the reliability floor.
Placement, diagnostics, repair, redundancy, and qualification must be designed together.

slides.title: Check Your Model: Reliability and Repair
slides.subtitle: Submit both questions for feedback. Correct answers are not required, and retries are available.

questions.prompt: Why is a direct replacement of every copper link with a conventional retimed optical module unsuitable for scale-up?

choices.text: The module count multiplies power and FIT into unacceptable rack-level totals

choices.feedback_incorrect: The issue is not fiber bandwidth. It is multiplying conventional module power and failure rates across the rack.

choices.text: Scale-up traffic never uses forward error correction
choices.feedback_incorrect: Scale-up links do use error detection and recovery. The direct-substitution problem is system power and reliability.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. More than a thousand conventional modules turn ordinary component values into severe rack penalties.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Return to the 72-accelerator example and multiply the module count by module power and FIT.

questions.prompt: Which measures improve availability for optics placed behind the front panel?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Availability combines prevention, diagnosis, and recovery.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Behind-panel optics need stronger qualification, not less. Add diagnostics, resiliency, and temperature control.

modules.title: Choosing an Optical Architecture and Roadmap
modules.subtitle: Placement, signaling, switching, deployment readiness, and ecosystem action.

slides.title: Choosing an Optical Architecture and Roadmap
slides.subtitle: Placement, signaling, switching, deployment readiness, and ecosystem action.

slides.title: Tradeoffs and Roadmaps You Will Compare
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module, you will be able to…
objectives: Compare pluggable, near-package, co-packaged, and slow-and-wide optical approaches.
Explain the paper's two-tier near-term deployment model.
Describe the role of optical circuit switching in a programmable scale-up fabric.
Evaluate PAM4, slow-and-wide optics, and short-reach copper at the 400G roadmap boundary.
Identify the coordinated ecosystem actions required for broad adoption.

slides.title: Placement Options Span Serviceable to Fully Integrated
slides.subtitle: Paper values are directional system estimates, not guaranteed product specifications.

slides.title: No Placement Wins Every System Tradeoff
slides.subtitle: The correct answer depends on the constraint the deployment cannot relax.

cards.title: Power
cards.body: Moving conversion toward the ASIC reduces electrical loss and equalization.

cards.title: Serviceability
cards.body: Front-panel modules minimize field-repair scope and downtime.

cards.title: Density
cards.body: NPO and CPO better match package escape and faceplate pressure.

cards.title: Reliability evidence
cards.body: New dense solutions need field data and qualification before scale-up deployment.

cards.title: Supply chain
cards.body: Tighter integration can concentrate sourcing and interoperability risk.

cards.title: Repair cost
cards.body: Behind-panel failures can require board, package, or factory-level replacement.

slides.title: Near-Term Deployment Follows a Two-Tier Path

figure.alt: Serviceability-first LPO and RTLR deployment transitioning toward NPO and CPO as reliability and standards mature
figure.caption: The paper favors an accessible optical entry point now, followed by deeper integration when field evidence and open interfaces reduce deployment risk.

slides.title: Optical Circuit Switching Makes Connectivity Programmable

bullets.text: OCS preserves a dedicated optical path instead of buffering and retransmitting packets.
Fiber-level paths can right-size hardware to a job or route around failures.
The link must absorb switch insertion loss, crosstalk, speed, scale, and technology-specific constraints.

figure.alt: Silent animation comparing optical-electrical-optical termination in an electrical switch with a continuous optical circuit that reconfigures from endpoint B to endpoint C
figure.caption: OCS removes intermediate electrical I/O from the data path, but makes optical switch loss part of the end-to-end link budget.

slides.title: At 400G per Lane, Optics Favors PAM4

bullets.text: Transmitter and material bandwidth become harder as the symbol rate rises.
Higher modulation order requires more received optical power for a given BER or SNR.
RIN, shot noise, interferometric noise, and return-loss sensitivity penalize PAM6 and PAM8.

figure.alt: Comparison showing PAM4 as more tractable for 400G optical signaling than PAM6 or PAM8
figure.caption: Copper benefits from lower Nyquist frequency at higher modulation order; optics pays a steeper noise and margin penalty.

slides.title: Slow-and-Wide Offers Another Scaling Direction

bullets.text: NRZ lanes reduce modulation bandwidth and can broaden the set of viable photonic technologies.
Multiple wavelengths on a fiber recover aggregate bandwidth without one extremely fast optical lane.
More lanes or wavelengths shift pressure toward fiber management, connector density, and optical routing.

figure.alt: Silent animation comparing one stressed high-rate optical lane with four slower NRZ lanes mapped to wavelengths and combined by WDM onto one fiber
figure.caption: Slow-and-wide optics trades lane speed for parallelism, using more electrical lanes and wavelengths to reach the same aggregate pipe.

slides.title: Copper May Persist at 400G—Over a Much Shorter Reach

bullets.text: Co-packaged copper minimizes die, package, and board loss before the cable begins.
A 448 Gb/s PAM4 analysis suggests about 1 m may be possible under strong technology assumptions.
The paper treats 0.5 m as a more realistic speculative reach while package and SerDes improvements remain uncertain.

figure.alt: Co-packaged copper path showing a shrinking practical reach from one meter toward half a meter at 448 gigabits per second
figure.caption: Copper remains valuable at the shortest tier, but the reach envelope contracts as the lane rate advances.

slides.title: The Roadmap Must Optimize the Whole System
items: Use LPO or RTLR when serviceability is the first deployment constraint.
Move toward NPO or CPO as field reliability and open interfaces mature.
Treat OCS as a programmable-fabric option with its own optical budget.
Keep both fast PAM4 and slow-and-wide WDM paths open while 400G technology matures.
Coordinate reach classes, qualification tiers, interface objectives, and protocol roadmaps.

slides.title: Check Your Model: Architecture and Ecosystem
slides.subtitle: Submit both questions for feedback. Correct answers are not required, and retries are available.

questions.prompt: Which option best matches a near-term deployment where field serviceability is the top priority?

choices.feedback_incorrect: CPO can improve power and signal integrity, but it raises the field-repair scope.
Slow-and-wide approaches remain promising but need a mature manufacturing and connector ecosystem.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The paper identifies LPO and RTLR as the accessible serviceability-first entry point.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Start with the paper's two-tier recommendation and the repair path of each option.

questions.prompt: Which actions support broad SROI adoption?

choices.text: Define intra-rack and inter-rack optical reach categories
Align interoperable optical objectives with scale-up protocol roadmaps
Require every protocol to use a different optical physical layer

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Common objectives let standards and suppliers aggregate volume across protocol families.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Fragmented protocol-specific optics work against the volume, cost, and reliability goals of SROI.
